title: CLES-FACIL Rocket Design
text:
Preface
Welcome to the CLES-FACIL Rocket Design technical manual.
This repository serves as an interactive reference and tutorial guide for rocket design, created for members of the CLES-FACIL association (cles-facil.org).

title: CLES-FACIL Rocket Design
text:
About This Manual
Our goal is to provide clear, interactive, and highly visual explanations of complex rocketry concepts, inspired by modern interactive textbooks. Whether you are a beginner looking to understand the basics of aerodynamics, or an advanced member working on structural optimization, you will find useful resources here.

title: CLES-FACIL Rocket Design
text:
Contents
Currently, this manual covers:

Fin Design & Stability: Understand fin geometry, the Barrowman equations, and compute your rocket’s stability margin through interactive calculators and visualizations.

More chapters on propulsion, recovery systems, and structures will be added soon.

title: 1  Fin Design & Stability Fundamentals
text:
1.1 Introduction
Fins are the primary means of ensuring passive aerodynamic stability on a rocket. When a rocket flies at a small angle of attack \(\alpha\) (i.e., it is slightly tilted relative to its velocity vector), aerodynamic forces act on its surfaces. Fins, placed at the rear of the rocket, generate a restoring moment that rotates the rocket back toward its flight path — much like the feathers on an arrow.
The key to understanding stability lies in two points:
The Barrowman equations (1966) provide an analytical method to compute the CP location for slender, finned rockets at small angles of attack. The specific formulas depend on the fin planform geometry chosen.

title: 1  Fin Design & Stability Fundamentals
text:
Center of Gravity (CG): the point where the rocket’s mass is balanced. This is the pivot point around which the rocket rotates.
Center of Pressure (CP): the point where the resultant of all aerodynamic normal forces acts.







ImportantThe Stability Rule



For a rocket to be statically stable, the Center of Pressure must be located behind (aft of) the Center of Gravity. The distance between them, expressed in body diameters (calibers), is called the stability margin:
\[
\text{Stability Margin} = \frac{X_{CP} - X_{CG}}{d}
\]
A stability margin of 1.0 to 2.0 calibers is generally considered ideal for model rockets. Less than 1.0 caliber is marginally stable; less than 0.5 is unstable.

TipRule of Thumb



For a first rocket, clipped delta or trapezoidal fins offer the best compromise. title: 1  Fin Design & Stability Fundamentals
text:
1.4 Barrowman Framework Overview
Regardless of fin shape, the Barrowman method computes two quantities for each rocket component:

Normal force coefficient derivative \(C_{N\alpha}\) — how much restoring force the component generates per radian of angle of attack
Center of pressure position \(X_{CP}\) — where that force effectively acts

The total rocket CP is the \(C_{N\alpha}\)-weighted average of all component CPs:
\[
X_{CP,\text{total}} = \frac{\displaystyle\sum_i C_{N\alpha,i}\,X_{CP,i}}{\displaystyle\sum_i C_{N\alpha,i}}
\]
The specific formulas for \(C_{N\alpha}\) and \(X_{CP}\) depend on the fin geometry. The following chapters derive them for:

Trapezoidal fins — the general case covering rectangular, delta, and clipped-delta planforms
Elliptical fins — requiring dedicated integral derivations

title: 1  Fin Design & Stability Fundamentals
text:
1.5 Assumptions & Limitations
The Barrowman method is valid under the following assumptions:

Small angle of attack — the rocket flies at \(\alpha < 10°\), where normal force varies linearly with \(\alpha\).
Subsonic, incompressible flow — Mach number \(Ma < 0.4\). No compressibility corrections are applied.
Slender, axisymmetric body — the rocket is long and thin relative to its diameter.
Sharp nose cone — blunt nose shapes may shift the CP forward from predicted values.
No body lift — the standard Barrowman method neglects lift generated by the body tube itself. Modified methods (Galejs, Rogers) account for this.
Rigid structure — no aeroelastic deformation of fins or body is considered.







TipFurther Reading




Barrowman, J.S. & Barrowman, J.A., “The Theoretical Prediction of the Center of Pressure”, 1966 — the original paper.
Nakka Rocketry — Barrowman Equations — excellent reference with worked examples.
RocketMime — Stability Calculator — another clear derivation.
RocketPy — Elliptical Fins Equations — derivations for elliptical planforms.

title: 2  Trapezoidal Fins — Barrowman Equations
text:
2.1 Introduction
The trapezoidal planform is the most general fin shape in rocketry. It is fully defined by four parameters, and encompasses several common geometries as special cases:
The Barrowman equations derived below apply to all of these shapes.

title: 2  Trapezoidal Fins — Barrowman Equations
text:
Rectangular fins: \(C_t = C_r\), \(\ell_m = 0\) (taper ratio \(\lambda = 1\))
Delta (triangular) fins: \(C_t = 0\) (\(\lambda = 0\))
Clipped delta fins: \(0 < C_t < C_r\), typical sweep (\(0 < \lambda < 1\))

title: 2  Trapezoidal Fins — Barrowman Equations
2  Trapezoidal Fins — Barrowman Equations
text:
2.3 Barrowman Equations
The Barrowman method computes two quantities for each rocket component: the normal force coefficient derivative \(C_{N\alpha}\) and the center of pressure \(X_{CP}\). For a set of trapezoidal fins, the key equations are:

2.3.1 Fin Planform Area
\[
A_f = \frac{C_r + C_t}{2} \cdot s
\]


2.3.2 Mid-Chord Line Length
The mid-chord line connects the midpoints of the root and tip chords. Its length governs the effective sweep:
\[
\ell_{mc} = \sqrt{s^2 + \left(\ell_m + \frac{C_t - C_r}{2}\right)^2}
\]


2.3.3 Normal Force Coefficient Derivative
For a set of \(N\) fins on a body of diameter \(d\):
\[
(C_{N\alpha})_F = \frac{4\,N\,(s/d)^2}{1 + \sqrt{1 + \left(\dfrac{2\,\ell_{mc}}{C_r + C_t}\right)^2}}
\]
This equation tells us how much restoring force the fins generate per radian of angle of attack. Higher values mean the fins are more effective at keeping the rocket aligned.


2.3.4 Fin-Body Interference Factor
The presence of the body tube accelerates airflow near the fin roots, increasing their effective lift. For 3 or 4 fins:
\[
K_{fb} = 1 + \frac{R}{s + R}
\]
where \(R = d/2\) is the body radius. The corrected coefficient is:
\[
(C_{N\alpha})_F^{\text{corrected}} = (C_{N\alpha})_F \cdot K_{fb}
\]


2.3.5 Fin Set Center of Pressure
The CP of the fin set, measured from the fin root leading edge:
\[
X_f = \frac{\ell_m\,(C_r + 2\,C_t)}{3\,(C_r + C_t)} + \frac{1}{6}\left(C_r + C_t - \frac{C_r\,C_t}{C_r + C_t}\right)
\]
To get the CP measured from the nose tip, add the distance from the nose tip to the fin root leading edge (\(X_{fLE}\)):
\[
X_{CP,\text{fins}} = X_{fLE} + X_f
\]

title: 3  Elliptical Fins — Theory & Equations
text:
3.1 Introduction
An elliptical fin planform produces the theoretically minimum induced drag for a given span and lift — the same principle behind the Supermarine Spitfire’s famous elliptical wing. In rocketry, elliptical fins are used on competition rockets where drag optimization matters.
Unlike trapezoidal fins, an elliptical fin is defined by only two parameters:
All other geometric properties are derived from the ellipse equation.

title: 3  Elliptical Fins — Theory & Equations
text:
Root chord (\(C_r\)): the chord at the body tube
Span (\(s\)): the radial extent of the fin








Note



The derivations in this chapter follow the RocketPy elliptical fins documentation, based on the Barrowman method.

title: 3  Elliptical Fins — Theory & Equations
3  Elliptical Fins — Theory & Equations
text:
3.3 Center of Pressure
For an elliptical fin, the center of pressure along the rocket centerline is located at a fixed fraction of the root chord, per the Model Rocket Technical Report:
\[
X_{CP} = 0.288 \, C_r
\]
measured aft from the fin root leading edge. From the nose tip:
\[
X_{CP,\text{fins}} = X_{fLE} + 0.288\,C_r
\]






Tip



This is notably simpler than the trapezoidal formula — the elliptical shape’s symmetry yields a clean constant.

title: 3  Elliptical Fins — Theory & Equations
text:
3.4 Normal Force Coefficient Derivative
For elliptical fins, the Barrowman \(C_{N\alpha}\) formula adapts by treating the effective geometry. Since the “tip chord” is zero and the planform tapers smoothly, the mid-chord line concept is replaced by an equivalent approach.
The effective calculation uses the same Barrowman framework with \(C_t = 0\) and an effective sweep derived from the ellipse geometry:
\[
(C_{N\alpha})_F = \frac{4\,N\,(s/d)^2}{1 + \sqrt{1 + \left(\dfrac{2\,s}{C_r}\right)^2}}
\]
With the fin-body interference factor:
\[
K_{fb} = 1 + \frac{R}{s + R}
\]
\[
(C_{N\alpha})_F^{\text{corrected}} = (C_{N\alpha})_F \cdot K_{fb}
\]

title: 3  Elliptical Fins — Theory & Equations
text:
3.5 Roll Damping Interference Factor
The roll damping interference factor for elliptical fins requires evaluating integrals over the elliptical chord distribution. The result is piecewise, depending on the ratio of span to body radius.
Let \(r = d/2\) be the body radius. According to Barrowman (via RocketPy):
When \(s > r\):
The interference factor involves both the body-immersed and free-stream portions of the fin, yielding a closed-form expression with inverse trigonometric terms.
When \(s < r\):
The fin is “short” relative to the body. The expressions simplify but remain dependent on the \(s/r\) ratio.
When \(s = r\):
The limiting case where both expressions converge.






Note



The full piecewise expressions are lengthy and best implemented computationally. They are documented in the RocketPy source code. Roll moment calculations using these factors will be covered in a dedicated Roll Dynamics chapter.
